Q23.text: I'm a late-stage graduate student, so my use of social media platforms is different than that of established PIs. I use Twitter and Facebook for sharing content, but also for learning about science that is OUTSIDE of my field. For example, by following the Scientific Reports twitter account, I saw an article and learned about plants responding to tactile stimuli. I'm a human physiology researcher, but the larger my breadth of knowledge, the more things I can draw upon for my future studies! These are things that I would not normally find by digging around on PubMed (which is also becoming a social site itself with comments, etc). Social media also serves to show me content that lots of people are talking about, particularly for hot topics like CRISPR. /  / In addition, I use social media for outreach. For over a year, I served as a social media manager for a fledgling public science outreach group that aimed to bring science from real scientists to middle and high school students though a variety of ways, but also to adults through science cafes. Our social media presence is why the group grew and later got absorbed by a larger outreach group, and I found that the public was actually seeking groups like us to learn from. People LIKE talking to scientists, but they don't know how to get to us, and are often intimidated because of the stigma behind being a scientist. They don't get that we're just normal people who do science. Social media is a highly effective platform to address science to the public, and it can be done in ways that are not intimidating to the public, but only if it is done correctly. That is something I'm happy to discuss if there is any way to link information. This makes social media highly important for my career as a scientist; so long as there is fear, miscommunication, and distance between scientists and the public, we're going to have a hard time moving forward. Thus, by being one of the people who tries to take science to nonscientists in a fun and inviting way, I'm helping my career and that of others... and having fun doing so!

Q23.text: Science communication and public outreach are HUGE for me — I actually manage the social media presence for a public science group, so a big chunk of my time goes into translating complex research into something a general audience can genuinely engage with and get excited about. Twitter and Facebook have been invaluable for that, not just as broadcast tools but as two-way conversations where members of the public ask questions and push back in ways that honestly sharpen my own thinking about my work. I also use social media heavily to follow researchers OUTSIDE my immediate field — physiology connects to so much (nutrition, neuroscience, exercise science, medicine) and Twitter in particular lets me stay across conversations I'd never encounter in a PubMed search alone. That kind of cross-disciplinary browsing has fed directly back into my PhD more than once, which I find really useful and kind of underrated as a benefit of these platforms!

Q29.text: Social media has been genuinely transformative for how I stay current with research — and I don't say that lightly. Twitter in particular functions almost like a live-updating journal club where I can follow not just the published papers but the conversations AROUND them: the debates, the replication attempts, the methodological critiques that never make it into the paper itself. That kind of behind-the-scenes scientific discourse is incredibly valuable for a PhD student trying to understand not just what findings are emerging but how science actually works as a process. I've also found that the cross-disciplinary reach is something traditional academic resources genuinely cant match — PubMed is great for finding literature in my field, but Twitter is where I discover that a nutritional biochemist or a sleep researcher is working on something that maps perfectly onto a question I've been wrestling with. And honestly, the public engagement dimension feeds back into research support too: when I'm explaining physiology concepts to a general audience and they push back with questions I haven't considered, it sharpens my own understanding in ways that feel REAL in a way that writing for peer review alone doesn't always do.

Q37.text: Sharing professional content through social media has genuinely changed what "dissemination" means to me — it's no longer just uploading a PDF to ResearchGate and hoping someone stumbles across it. Twitter and Facebook let you actively PUSH findings into conversations where they're relevant, and more importantly, you can share them in forms that are accessible to people who would never read the journal article itself. I think this is CRITICALLY important for publicly-funded research: if our work matters, we have an obligation to make it legible beyond the paywall and beyond the jargon. I've had moments where I share a simplified thread about a physiology concept and the response from the public is enormous — people are genuinely hungry for this kind of content, and that's not something you'd ever know if you only published through traditional venues. The challenge, honestly, is that most researchers haven't been trained to translate their work for a general audience, and social media almost forces you to develop that skill because you lose people immediately if you lean too heavily on technical language. I find that constraint incredibly useful for my own development as a scientist and communicator — it makes you interrogate what you actually understand versus what you can only describe in field-specific shorthand.

Q43.text: Promotion is where I think social media really separates itself from traditional academic channels in a way that's almost impossible to overstate. When I publish something — or when someone in my network does — the ability to actually DRIVE people toward that work, rather than passively hoping it gets discovered, is a fundamentally different model of academic communication. Twitter in particular lets you frame why a piece of work matters, who it's relevant to, and what question it's answering before someone even clicks the link — that context is half the battle when you're competing for attention in an information-saturated environment. I've watched relatively niche physiology papers get genuinely wide traction because someone took the time to explain in plain language why the finding was surprising or important, and that promotional effort clearly came from the researcher themselves, not a PR department. And honestly I think that's the right model — researchers are the best advocates for their own work, they just need platforms that let them speak directly to audiences without institutional gatekeeping. What I find really exciting is that social media collapses the distance between "promotion to peers" and "promotion to the public" — the same tweet can reach a cardiologist AND a curious person who just wants to understand how their heart works, and that dual reach is something no traditional dissemination channel has ever managed. The only real limitation I'd flag is that promotional success on these platforms does reward a certain kind of personality and time investment that not everyone can offer equally, which is worth acknowledging as a structural issue for how we think about visibility in academia.

Q47.text: Networking is honestly where I've had some of the most unexpected and exciting outcomes from social media — connections that would simply never have happened through conventional academic channels. Twitter in particular has this remarkable ability to collapse hierarchies that normally make it very difficult for a PhD student to get on the radar of established researchers: if you engage thoughtfully with someone's work publicly, they can see that and respond, and suddenly you're in a genuine intellectual exchange with someone whose papers you've been citing for years. That kind of lateral access is almost UNHEARD of in traditional academic networking, where geography and institutional prestige do so much of the filtering. I've made connections with researchers in exercise science, neuroscience, and nutrition — fields that touch my own work in physiology but that I'd have very little formal contact with otherwise — and a couple of those Twitter exchanges have evolved into real conversations about research directions and potential collaboration. It doesn't always lead somewhere, but the batting average is way higher than cold-emailing someone whose paper you admired. What I also find really valuable is that the networking isn't purely transactional — following researchers in adjacent fields and watching how they frame problems and methodological choices has shaped how I think about my own work in ways that are hard to quantify but feel genuinely significant. And honestly, running social media for a public science group has extended that network beyond academia altogether, connecting me with science communicators, journalists, and educators whose perspective on how research lands with a general audience is something I couldn't get from any SCN platform alone. That combination — peer networking AND public-facing networking through the same tools — is something I find really hard to replicate anywhere else

Q63.text:
The single biggest thing publishers could do — and this feels almost embarrassingly obvious — is make open access the DEFAULT rather than the expensive exception. Right now when I share a paper on Twitter and someone from the general public clicks the link, they hit a paywall, and that's the moment the whole exercise collapses. You've done the hard work of translating research into something accessible and interesting, and then the publisher slams a door in their face. It undermines everything social media can do for dissemination in a really fundamental way, and I find it honestly pretty maddening.

Beyond that, I'd love to see publishers invest seriously in lay summaries — not as an afterthought, but as a genuine deliverable required at submission and written by the authors themselves rather than a PR team that doesn't understand the science. A well-written plain-language summary sitting alongside every article would give researchers who WANT to share their work something concrete and pre-approved to build from. Graphical abstracts that are actually designed to be shared on social platforms (not just squashed into a journal sidebar) would help too.

And honestly, I think publishers should be actively TRAINING researchers in science communication as part of publication support — workshops, resources, even just clear guidance on how to translate findings for a general audience. There is an enormous appetite out there for accessible science and publishers are sitting on a goldmine of content they're doing almost nothing to help researchers activate. That gap between what exists in journals and what the public can actually reach and understand feels like one of the most solvable problems in academic communication right now, if publishers were willing to treat it as their problem too.

Q65.text:
I just want to say that filling out this survey has actually made me reflect on how much my professional identity has been shaped by social media in ways that feel almost impossible to separate out now — it's not a tool I USE for research, it's become part of how I THINK about research, how I communicate it, and why I do it. That probably sounds grandiose but I mean it genuinely.

The one thing I haven't had a chance to say anywhere in this survey is how frustrating it is that none of this engagement counts for anything in formal academic assessment. I spend real time and creative energy on science communication through Twitter and Facebook, I've built an audience of people who are genuinely interested in physiology, and that labour is essentially invisible when it comes to how a PhD student is evaluated or how a researcher is hired. That structural mismatch feels like a real problem — institutions SAY they value public engagement but the incentive architecture doesn't reflect that at all, and until it does, a lot of researchers who might otherwise lean into social media are going to keep treating it as a guilty pleasure rather than a legitimate part of their professional contribution.

If this survey shapes any policy thinking at Springer Nature I'd really love for that tension to be part of the conversation. The platforms exist, the public appetite exists — what's missing is institutional permission to take it seriously.

Q23.label: Are there any other tasks you use social media/ SCN for, in relation to your work?
Q23.text: I'm a late-stage graduate student, so my use of social media platforms is different than that of established PIs. I use Twitter and Facebook for sharing content, but also for learning about science that is OUTSIDE of my field. For example, by following the Scientific Reports twitter account, I saw an article and learned about plants responding to tactile stimuli. I'm a human physiology researcher, but the larger my breadth of knowledge, the more things I can draw upon for my future studies! These are things that I would not normally find by digging around on PubMed (which is also becoming a social site itself with comments, etc). Social media also serves to show me content that lots of people are talking about, particularly for hot topics like CRISPR. /  / In addition, I use social media for outreach. For over a year, I served as a social media manager for a fledgling public science outreach group that aimed to bring science from real scientists to middle and high school students though a variety of ways, but also to adults through science cafes. Our social media presence is why the group grew and later got absorbed by a larger outreach group, and I found that the public was actually seeking groups like us to learn from. People LIKE talking to scientists, but they don't know how to get to us, and are often intimidated because of the stigma behind being a scientist. They don't get that we're just normal people who do science. Social media is a highly effective platform to address science to the public, and it can be done in ways that are not intimidating to the public, but only if it is done correctly. That is something I'm happy to discuss if there is any way to link information. This makes social media highly important for my career as a scientist; so long as there is fear, miscommunication, and distance between scientists and the public, we're going to have a hard time moving forward. Thus, by being one of the people who tries to take science to nonscientists in a fun and inviting way, I'm helping my career and that of others... and having fun doing so!
